claims.text: A Service's cluster IP is a virtual address that no single host answers. On donhang (iptables mode) no Pod and no node holds it; it is only the destination kube-proxy's rules match. kubectl get pods/nodes -o wide list Pod and node addresses.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Services > Virtual IPs and Service Proxies ('Service IPs are not actually answered by a single host'); Service > ClusterIP

claims.text: kube-proxy runs on every node, watches Services and EndpointSlices through the API server, and writes on its node rules that redirect connections for a Service's cluster IP and port to one of the Service's ready Pods.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies (overview, iptables proxy mode); Reference > Command line tools > kube-proxy

claims.text: An EndpointSlice, kept by the control plane for a Service with a selector, lists the addresses of the Pods the selector matches and each endpoint's ready condition; it is updated when Pods start, stop or change readiness. It carries the label kubernetes.io/service-name.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Services > EndpointSlices (Conditions: ready; Ownership: kubernetes.io/service-name label)

claims.text: Normally only ready endpoints get new connections: kube-proxy writes no forwarding entry for a Pod that is not ready (terminating-endpoint fallback is out of scope; the lesson says 'normally').
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: EndpointSlices > Conditions (ready = serving and not terminating; proxies normally ignore terminating endpoints)

claims.text: In the kind cluster donhang, kube-proxy runs in iptables mode ('mode: iptables' in the kube-proxy ConfigMap's config.conf). Each kind node is a Docker container, so docker exec donhang-worker runs a command on that node.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/kube-proxy.txt ('mode: iptables'); kind docs: Quick Start (nodes are Docker containers)

claims.text: In iptables mode kube-proxy's rules match packets for the cluster IP and port, then hold one entry per endpoint picked at random, and each entry rewrites the destination (DNAT) to the Pod's address and targetPort. Chain names are not taught (depth_notes).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies > iptables proxy mode ('selects a backend at random'); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/kube-proxy.txt

claims.text: With two endpoints, the first KUBE-SVC entry is taken with probability 0.5 and the second takes the rest, so each Pod gets about half of new connections.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/kube-proxy.txt (--probability 0.50000000000, second line unconditional)

claims.text: The rules apply to the first packet of a connection; the node's kernel keeps a record of each open connection and its chosen backend, so later packets go to the same Pod: the Pod is chosen once per connection, not per request.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies > iptables proxy mode; outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/kube-proxy.txt ('answers: 10, different Pods that answered: 1')

claims.text: In iptables mode, after the destination is rewritten, packets travel over the Pod network like any Pod-to-Pod packet; kube-proxy is not on the data path (the lesson scopes this to donhang).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies > iptables proxy mode (rules in kernel netfilter; packets redirected to the backend); Glossary > kube-proxy

claims.text: HTTP/1.1 lets a client send several requests over one kept-open (persistent) connection; a request with 'Connection: close' asks the server to close the connection after its response.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9112 §9.3 Persistence, §9.6 Tear-down (refs/rfc)

claims.text: Each wget in the loop is a new process and opens its own connection, so ten wget calls are ten connections; in the captured run both Pods answered (different Pods that answered: 2).
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang scripts/k8s/kube-proxy.sh lines 33-38 and outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/kube-proxy.txt

claims.text: A headless Service (clusterIP: None) gets no kube-proxy rules; its clients get Pod addresses from cluster DNS and connect directly. Captured: echo-ip-headless CLUSTER-IP None, 0 rules on donhang-worker.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Services > Headless Services ('kube-proxy does not handle these Services'); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/kube-proxy.txt

claims.text: kube-proxy has proxy modes other than iptables, and some CNI plugins replace kube-proxy with eBPF programs in the kernel; the node then holds different rules or programs, but a connection to the cluster IP is still sent to one of the Service's ready Pods.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies > Proxy modes; Cluster Administration > Addons / Networking (kube-proxy replacement)

claims.text: eBPF loads small programs into the Linux kernel; some CNI plugins use it to handle Service connections in place of kube-proxy's rules.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Cluster Administration > Addons (Cilium: eBPF-based data plane, kube-proxy replacement); glossary ebpf short_en

claims.text: iptables keeps packet rules in the Linux kernel; iptables-save -t nat prints the nat table's rules, and kube-proxy tags each of its rules with a comment (removed by the script's sed).
claims.source_hint: iptables-save(8) man page (no docs root in versions.yaml; behaviour visible in outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/kube-proxy.txt)

claims.text: echo-ip Service: port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=echo-ip; EndpointSlice output shows two ready addresses with port 8080. Each echo-ip answer is one line: '<Pod name> saw <remote address>' (Caddyfile respond).
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang deploy/k8s/lessons/echo-ip.yaml and outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/kube-proxy.txt at stage-3

claims.text: show (scripts/lib/network-lessons.sh) prints a command after '$' then runs it; kube-proxy.sh rebuilds the cluster donhang first if it is gone (lessons_cluster).
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang scripts/lib/network-lessons.sh at stage-3 (same as k8s.l3.cni-plugins claims 14-15)

claims.text: Clients holding long-lived connections stay on the Pod picked when they connected, so Pods added later get no traffic from those connections and load can be uneven.
claims.source_hint: follows from claim 8; kubernetes.io: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies (per-connection backend selection)

claims.text: A message broker decides which consumer gets each message, while a Service's choice is made once per connection.
claims.source_hint: rabbitmq.com/docs: Consumers (messages delivered to consumers of a queue); lesson backend.l3.message-broker

claims.text: NodePort and LoadBalancer traffic goes through the same kube-proxy rules as cluster IP traffic.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies > iptables Example ('This same basic flow executes when traffic comes in through a type: NodePort Service, or through a load-balancer')
